# Every prompt this experiment sends

Reproduced verbatim from the source, because "the only difference between the two
agents is a memory layer" is a claim about prompts, and a reader should be able to
check it without reading Python. `tests/test_prompts.py` fails if this file drifts
from the code.

There are four model calls in the experiment, and only **one** of them differs
between the agents — and it differs only in which context blocks are present:

| Phase | Who runs it | Prompt |
|---|---|---|
| `review` | **both agents** | the same frozen `SYSTEM_PROMPT` below |
| `prime`  | memory agent only, once per repo | `PRIMER_SYSTEM` |
| `write`  | memory agent only, after each review | `WRITE_SYSTEM` |
| `retrieve` | memory agent only | not a model call — a store search; the query text is below |

## The confound this design is guarding

The review system prompt is **byte-identical for both agents**, and it names the
optional `Prior knowledge` section explicitly. That is deliberate: if the prompt
described only the sections a given agent supplies, the two agents would send
different bytes, and every token comparison would be confounded by prompt length
as well as by prompt content. Instead, both agents send the same instructions and
the *presence or absence of blocks* is the whole difference.

## 1. `review` — the shared system prompt (both agents)

Sent by the baseline and the memory agent, unchanged, on every PR. `reviewbot/review.py::SYSTEM_PROMPT`.

```text
You are reviewing a pull request against a Python library that other software depends on at runtime. Report defects a maintainer would act on.

You may be given some or all of the following, in this order:
- Repo conventions: a contributor guide or distilled conventions for this repository.
- Prior knowledge: durable facts about this repo, past review findings, and review policy. This section may be absent. When it is present, treat it as established context and do not re-derive it; when it is absent, work from the source provided.
- Source context: the current contents of files the change touches. This section may be absent.
- The diff: the change under review, as unified patches per file.

Rules for findings:
- Report only defects introduced or left unaddressed by this diff. Do not report pre-existing issues in unchanged code, and do not restate what the diff already does correctly.
- Anchor every finding to a file and, where the patch makes it determinable, a line.
- Prefer one precise finding over three speculative ones. If you are not confident a reader would agree it is a defect, either omit it or mark confidence low.
- Style points are findings only when they violate a stated convention.
- If the change is clean, return an empty findings list. An empty review is a valid review.

If a Prior knowledge section is present, list in `memories_used` the id of every item you actually relied on. Do not list items you were merely shown.
```

### The user-turn blocks, in order

`build_request()` assembles these. The prompt-cache breakpoint sits at the end of the last **stable** block, so the conventions are cached and the per-PR material is not.

| # | Block | baseline | memory agent |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | `Repo conventions:` (stable, cached) | yes | yes |
| 2 | `Prior knowledge:` (retrieved memories) | **never** | when retrieval returns anything |
| 3 | `Source context:` (full text of touched files) | **every PR** | never |
| 4 | `The diff:` (unified patches) | yes | yes |


Block 2 versus block 3 *is* the experiment: the baseline re-reads source to rebuild its understanding of the repo, the memory agent reads a distilled slice of what was already understood.


Rendered shapes, from the block builders:

```text
Repo conventions:

===== CONTRIBUTING.md =====
<file text>

Source context:

===== redis/connection.py =====
<file text>

Prior knowledge:
[conv-redis-connection-py-socket-lifecycle] <one durable fact>
[find-redis-cluster-py-slot-cache-lock-7] <a past finding>
```

Memory ids are exposed in the `Prior knowledge` block on purpose: the model is asked to list the ones it relied on in `memories_used`, which is the retrieval-precision signal (spec §7b). Without the ids there is no way to tell 20-retrieved-3-used from 20-retrieved-20-used.

## 2. `prime` — building repo knowledge once (memory agent only)

One call per spine module, at `pr_ordinal=0`, before the sequence starts. Per-module rather than one big call so re-priming a single changed module does not re-pay for the rest. `reviewbot/agents.py::PRIMER_SYSTEM`.

```text
You are building a durable knowledge base about a Python library so that future code reviews do not have to re-read the whole module to understand it.

Read the module given to you and extract the facts a reviewer would otherwise have to re-derive every time they see a diff touching it: what the module is responsible for, the invariants callers depend on, the conventions the code follows, and the ownership boundaries between it and its neighbours.

Rules:
- One fact per record. A record that contains two facts cannot be invalidated independently when one of them changes.
- Write each fact so it is useful without the source in front of you. "Uses a lock" is useless; "every mutation of the slot cache must hold _lock, because concurrent MOVED handling races otherwise" is a fact a reviewer can act on.
- Prefer facts that would let a reviewer judge a diff: invariants, required call ordering, error-handling conventions, what must never happen.
- Do not describe individual functions line by line, do not restate the code, and do not include anything version-specific or dated.
- 8 to 20 records per module is the useful range. Fewer means you skipped things; more means you are transcribing.
```

```json
{
  "type": "object",
  "properties": {
    "facts": {
      "type": "array",
      "items": {
        "type": "object",
        "properties": {
          "topic": {
            "type": "string",
            "description": "2-5 word slug naming the fact, stable across re-primes"
          },
          "kind": {
            "type": "string",
            "enum": [
              "architecture",
              "convention",
              "invariant",
              "ownership"
            ]
          },
          "fact": {
            "type": "string"
          }
        },
        "required": [
          "topic",
          "kind",
          "fact"
        ],
        "additionalProperties": false
      }
    }
  },
  "required": [
    "facts"
  ],
  "additionalProperties": false
}
```

## 3. `write` — distilling findings into memories (memory agent only)

Runs after each review that produced findings. This is a **measured model call**, not free bookkeeping: its tokens are in the memory agent's column, which is why savings can be reported net of overhead. `--no-distill` swaps it for a zero-model-token variant that writes findings verbatim.

```text
You are recording what a code review learned, so that a future review of the same repository does not have to re-derive it.

You are given the findings from one review. Turn them into durable records. A record is worth writing only if it would change how a later review of *different* code in this repository behaves.

Rules:
- One fact per record, phrased as a reusable rule or a recurring pattern, not as a report about this specific diff. "PR 3411 leaked a socket" is useless; "connection setup in connection.py must close the socket if the handshake raises, this was missed once" is reusable.
- Skip findings that are purely local to the diff and teach nothing general.
- If a finding is an instance of a pattern likely to recur, say so in the pattern field.
- Return an empty list if the review taught nothing durable. That is a normal outcome.
- `module` must be copied verbatim from the `file` of one of the findings you were given. It is a retrieval key matched by exact string equality, not a description: any other value makes the record unreachable forever.
```

```json
{
  "type": "object",
  "properties": {
    "records": {
      "type": "array",
      "items": {
        "type": "object",
        "properties": {
          "module": {
            "type": "string"
          },
          "topic": {
            "type": "string"
          },
          "pattern": {
            "type": "string"
          },
          "text": {
            "type": "string"
          }
        },
        "required": [
          "module",
          "topic",
          "pattern",
          "text"
        ],
        "additionalProperties": false
      }
    }
  },
  "required": [
    "records"
  ],
  "additionalProperties": false
}
```

The `module` field is a **retrieval key matched by exact string equality**, not a description. A model-supplied value is resolved against the PR's touched files before it becomes a topic (`memory.resolve_modules`) — on the first real run, 5 of 6 written findings named a directory rather than a file and would have been unretrievable forever. See spec §4d.


## 4. `retrieve` — the search query (memory agent only)

Not a model call. The query text is built from the PR itself, and deliberately contains **no PR number and no timestamp**: it is prompt-adjacent, and an identifier in it would make retrieval incomparable across runs.

```python
f"{pr.title}. Files changed: {modules}"
```

Scoped by `filterOp: all` with `namespace eq`, `memoryType in [repo_convention, review_finding]`, and `topics in [touched files]`. The filter shape is load-bearing and non-obvious — see spec §4d and `reviewbot/memory.py`.


## What is NOT sent

- **No tools.** Neither agent has tool access; context is assembled by the harness, so token accounting is exact rather than dependent on what a model chose to fetch.
- **No assistant prefill.** It returns a 400 on this model; structured output comes from `output_config.format`.
- **No PR number, date, or run id anywhere in a cached prefix.** Any of those would silently zero the prompt cache, and a cache miss reads as context volume.
